newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Direct Taiwan-China sailing starts April 18-paper.
newsitem.headline: Direct Taiwan-China sailing starts April 18-paper.

text.p: The first ship in 48 years to cross the Taiwan strait directly will set sail from the Chinese mainland on Thursday for arrival in rival Taiwan's Kaohsiung port early on Friday, Taiwan media said.

The Sheng Da, owned by communist China's Fujian Provincial Shipping Co but registered in Saint Vincent, would leave Xiamen port in China's southeastern Fujian province, Taipei's China Times on Wednesday quoted mainland sources as saying.
Kaohsiung port officials reached by telephone said the Sheng Da had not yet given mandatory formal notice of its intent to enter the port.

The Sheng Da is one of four ships from four mainland sea freight firms approved by Taiwan on April 11 to sail directly into Kaohsiung from the mainland, cautiously easing a ban on direct links dating to a civil war that split them in 1949.

Nationalist-ruled Taiwan denies that the long-forbidden crossings are direct links because mainland cargoes will not be allowed to enter Taiwan customs. Rather, they can only be processed at what Taiwan is calling an "offshore transshipment centre" for onward shipment to third countries.
Likewise, Taiwan cargoes at Kaohsiung cannot be put aboard ships planning to cross directly to two mainland ports approved for the scheme -- Xiamen and the Fujian capital Fuzhou.
The four approved mainland shippers are Fujian Foreign Trade Centre Shipping Co, Fujian Provincial Shipping Co, Fujian Xiamen Shipping Co and Shamen Ocean Shipping Co.
A dozen Taiwan shipping companies were still awaiting word from Beijing on the fate of their bids to ply direct routes.
Analysts said Taiwan's Yangming Marine Transport Corp, Uniglory Marine, Wan Hai Lines and Chinese Maritime Transport Ltd were likely to be selected.

Taiwan proposed the offshore transshipment scheme in 1995 in a strategy to ensure direct crossings did not undermine the sovereignty of its exiled Republic of China, which fled to the island after being routed from the mainland in 1949.
Beijing, taking a different tack, says the routes are domestic links between two provinces, one of which, Taiwan, remains under control of a renegade government.
Taiwan still bans all direct contacts with the rival mainland, but faces huge pressure from Taiwan business circles to relax the ban.
Some 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured US$30 billion into mainland investments and say direct air, maritime and other links could trim needless costs of cultivating their China businesses.
